claims.text: Elevated intrinsic compressive residual stress governs the wear performance of CoCrFeMnNi coatings.
A high-energy deposition process induces higher intrinsic compressive residual stress in CoCrFeMnNi coatings.
Compressive residual stress impedes crack initiation and propagation during cyclic loading.
Compressive residual stress enhances work hardening during cyclic loading.
The baseline consists of conventionally deposited coatings with moderate or lower compressive residual stress.
High-energy pulsed laser deposition will produce greater compressive residual stress than conventional lower-energy deposition.
Deposition energy is intended to be the sole experimental variable between the two coating sets.
Residual compressive stress can be quantitatively measured using XRD sin²ψ.
Higher compressive residual stress redistributes contact loads.
Arrested microcracking, redistributed contact loads, and enhanced work hardening reduce coating wear.
High-energy-deposited coatings with higher compressive residual stress will have lower wear depths than baseline coatings.
High-energy-deposited coatings with higher compressive residual stress will have lower friction coefficients than baseline coatings.
High-energy-deposited coatings with higher compressive residual stress will develop fewer fatigue-induced microcracks than baseline coatings.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold under room-temperature cyclic wear conditions.
Uncontrolled differences in grain structure or texture may alter the apparent effect of residual stress on wear.
